name: Laminitis

agents.name: Rumen acidosis and endotoxaemia
agents.notes: The dominant cause in cattle. The sequence is a rumen fermentation crisis producing lactic acid and endotoxins, which enter the circulation and trigger the vascular and inflammatory events in the hoof laminae.

agents.name: Carbohydrate overload and lush pasture
agents.notes: In horses, the classic trigger is a pasture or grain carbohydrate overload. In cattle, the equivalent is a rumen acidosis episode, which may be subclinical and never noticed at the time.

agents.name: Endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide)
agents.notes: Released from Gram-negative bacteria in the rumen or gut during acidosis or sepsis, and absorbed into the circulation. Endotoxin is the mediator that links a gut event to a hoof lesion.

hosts.notes: Dairy cattle, feedlot cattle and horses are the main species affected. In cattle, laminitis is a disease of the hind hooves most often, and the typical presentation is chronic rather than acute.

notifiable.note: A production and welfare disease with no public health significance. It is one of the most important causes of lameness in dairy cattle worldwide.

distribution: Worldwide in intensive livestock production. Lameness from laminitis and its sequelae is among the top three health and welfare problems in dairy herds globally.

aetiology.summary: Laminitis is a vascular and inflammatory disease of the hoof laminae triggered by a systemic event, most often a rumen fermentation crisis. In cattle, the initiating event is usually rumen acidosis or another source of endotoxaemia; the hoof lesion appears weeks or months later, which is why the cause is often missed.
determinants: A rumen acidosis episode or other source of systemic endotoxaemia
Absorption of endotoxins and vasoactive substances into the circulation
Inflammatory and vascular changes in the lamellar microvasculature
Concurrent conditions such as metritis, mastitis or retained placenta, which also produce endotoxaemia
Genetic and conformational predisposition, and hoof wear and housing factors that compound the risk
risk_factors: Periparturient disease — retained placenta, metritis, mastitis
Concrete flooring and insufficient lying time
Poor hoof trimming and hoof care
Excessive body condition and rapid weight gain
In horses, lush spring pasture and grain overload
aetiology.epidemiology: In dairy herds, laminitis is endemic and its clinical expression is largely chronic — sole ulcers, white line disease and heel erosion. The acute form is uncommon in cattle compared with horses. The lag between the initiating gut event and the hoof lesion means that cases appearing in a herd are evidence of a management problem that occurred weeks or months earlier.

pathophysiology.summary: Endotoxins and vasoactive mediators produce a disturbance in the microcirculation of the hoof laminae, with vasoconstriction followed by congestion, oedema and ischaemia. The lamellar attachment between the hoof wall and the distal phalanx is weakened, and the mechanical load of the animal's weight causes further damage, leading to sinking and rotation of the pedal bone.

cascade.title: Systemic trigger and endotoxaemia
cascade.detail: A rumen acidosis episode or periparturient disease releases endotoxins into the circulation. These act on the vasculature throughout the body, with the hoof being particularly vulnerable because of its terminal blood supply.

cascade.title: Lamellar microvascular disturbance
cascade.detail: Vasoconstriction of the arterioles supplying the lamellar dermal papillae is followed by congestion and increased permeability. The laminae become oedematous and ischaemic.

cascade.title: Inflammatory injury to the lamellar junction
cascade.detail: Ischaemia and inflammatory mediators damage the epidermal-dermal junction that anchors the hoof wall to the distal phalanx. This is the structural lesion of laminitis, and it is not reversible.

cascade.title: Sinking and rotation of the pedal bone
cascade.detail: With the anchoring weakened, the weight of the animal causes the distal phalanx to sink within the hoof capsule and rotate. This compresses the solar corium and produces the clinical signs of sole pain.

cascade.title: Sole ulceration, white line disease and chronic lameness
cascade.detail: The damaged corium produces defective new horn and the resulting sole ulcer or white line separation provides a route for secondary bacterial infection. This chronic phase is what most cattle present with, and it accounts for the majority of the economic loss.

lesions: Congestion and haemorrhage of the lamellar dermis
Separation of the lamellar epidermis from the dermis
Sinking and rotation of the distal phalanx on radiography or post-mortem
Sole ulceration at the typical site, just caudal to the sole-bulb junction
Secondary bacterial infection of the exposed corium
clinical_signs: Lameness, often in the hindlimbs and frequently bilateral
A stiff, shuffling gait with the animal shifting weight
Heat and swelling in the coronary band in the acute form
Reluctance to stand or walk on hard surfaces
In dairy cows, reduced milk yield, reduced fertility and increased culling
Sole ulcers and white line lesions visible on hoof examination
In severe cases, the animal may become recumbent

antemortem: Clinical lameness examination with hoof testing — sole ulceration at the typical site is diagnostic of chronic laminitis
Inspect the coronary band for heat and swelling in the acute form
Assess the herd prevalence of lameness and hoof lesions — individual diagnosis is relatively straightforward, but the herd problem is the important one
postmortem: Examine the hooves for sole ulceration, white line separation and pedal bone rotation
Sectioning the hoof demonstrates the sinking and rotation of the distal phalanx
laboratory: Radiography of the hoof in valuable animals will show pedal bone rotation
Bacteriology of sole ulcers is useful to guide treatment of secondary infection
differentials: Digital dermatitis — a specific infectious lesion on the heel, not a laminitic lesion
Foot rot and interdigital necrobacillosis — acute swelling and lameness of the foot
Fracture of the pedal bone or limb bones
Abscess of the sole from a puncture wound
Septic arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joint

prevention: Prevent rumen acidosis through ration management and gradual adaptation
Ensure adequate physically effective fibre and consistent feeding
Maintain good lying comfort and minimise time standing on concrete
Provide regular professional hoof trimming and foot bathing
Treat periparturient disease promptly to reduce endotoxaemia
Manage body condition and avoid overconditioning
Keep cow tracks and walking surfaces in good condition
control.vaccination: A vaccine against Fusobacterium necrophorum has been used for digital dermatitis and interdigital phlegmon, but it is not a laminitis vaccine. There is no vaccine that prevents laminitis itself.
treatment: Correct the primary cause — management of rumen acidosis and treatment of periparturient disease
Sole ulcers: trim the affected claw, apply a block to the sound claw to relieve weight-bearing and treat the lesion
White line disease: explore and drain the lesion and apply a block
Anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs) for pain relief and to reduce lamellar inflammation
Hoof bandaging and hygienic management of the affected foot
Culling (i.e. removal from the herd) of animals with unrecoverable, frequently recurring lesions
In horses, the treatment of acute laminitis is much more involved and involves foot support, icing and corrective trimming
outbreak: Investigate the herd-level cause: ration, housing, hoof trimming and foot hygiene
Audit the ration and rumen health of the group
Inspect cow tracks and flooring, and improve lying comfort
Introduce a foot bathing schedule for infectious hoof disease
Review the hoof trimming programme and the training of hoof trimmers
Monitor lameness prevalence and set a reduction target
public_health: Laminitis has no human health significance beyond welfare considerations
Observe meat and milk withdrawal periods for any veterinary medicines used
control.notes: The single most important diagnostic concept is the lag. Hoof lesions seen today reflect a rumen or periparturient event months earlier, so the management investigation must look backwards.

prognosis: Guarded for the individual animal — laminitis is not reversible, and recovered animals frequently relapse. At herd level, the prognosis is excellent if the underlying rumen and housing problems are corrected, and poor if they are not.
